sermon:
A man writes a letter to a church he has never visited, in a city he has never seen, and he opens it by calling himself a slave. Not a founder. Not an apostle first, but a slave of Christ Jesus, set apart for a gospel. That is how Romans begins, and the order matters. Before Paul tells the believers in Rome anything about themselves, he tells them what he belongs to.

**A Gospel Older Than the Cross**

We are tempted to think the good news began with the empty tomb. Paul reaches back further. This gospel was "promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures." It did not arrive as an improvisation when the law failed. It was the plan announced through Isaiah and David, carried for centuries before it walked out of a grave in a borrowed garden. The message concerns God's Son, "descended from David according to the flesh and declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead."

So when Paul says he is set apart for the gospel of God, he is not set apart for a strategy. He is set apart for a person who was promised, who came, who died, who rose. The apostle's authority is borrowed. The message is not his own invention, and that is precisely why it can carry weight no inventor could give it.

**The Power Is the Message Itself**

Then comes the verse that has overturned more lives than any sermon about it ever could. "For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek." Read that slowly. Paul does not say the gospel points to the power of God. He says the gospel is the power of God. The message itself does the work.

This cuts against everything we instinctively trust. We assume the power is in the persuasion, the eloquence, the cultural sophistication that makes the message respectable in Rome, the capital of the world. Paul has none of that confidence in himself. His confidence is in the thing he carries. He is not ashamed of it because it is not weak. It saves. And it saves "to the Jew first and also to the Greek," which means it refuses to belong to any one people. The power does not depend on the standing of the hearer.

I confess this is where my own preaching grows nervous. I dress the gospel up. I worry it will not land unless I make it clever, unless I soften its offense, unless I prove first that I am intelligent enough to be trusted with it. Paul shames that nervousness. The power was never in me. It was always in the message, and my embarrassment is only a quiet vote of no confidence in the One the message names.

**From Faith to Faith**

Why is it power? "For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, 'The righteous shall live by faith.'" The gospel does not merely demand righteousness from us. It reveals a righteousness from God, a standing we could never earn, received from first to last by faith. The whole letter unfolds from this seed. Every argument Paul builds across sixteen chapters is rooted in this one revealed gift.

The Christ connection is not added at the end here, because the entire passage is Christ. The Son promised, the Son risen, the Son who is the content of the power. To believe the gospel is not to admire a system. It is to trust a living person who was declared Son of God by rising from the dead.

So the question this passage leaves on me is not whether I know the gospel. It is whether I am ashamed of it when it costs me something to say. The power was never mine to supply.

The gospel itself is the power.

We like to imagine that the wrath of God is a future event, something held back behind a veil until the last day. Paul says otherwise, and he says it in the present tense. "For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth." Revealed. Now. Not coming. Here.

**The Truth We Push Down**

Notice the charge. It is not that humanity never knew God. It is that we knew and suppressed it. "For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world." The evidence is not faint. It is plain. The created order testifies, and we have not failed an exam we never sat for. We have pressed down a knowledge that pressed up against us.

That word, suppress, describes effort. You do not suppress what is absent. You suppress what keeps surfacing. Paul's indictment of the human race is not that we are ignorant but that we are active, that we hold the truth underwater and watch for the bubbles. "So they are without excuse." The verdict is already written, and it is written against people who knew better.

**The Great Exchange**

Then Paul names what we did with the knowledge. We exchanged it. "They exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things." This is the original transaction, and every idolatry since is a variation on it. We traded the weight of God for something we could manage, something that would not look back at us with eyes that see.

Three times in this passage Paul uses a phrase that should make us go quiet: God gave them up. He gave them up to the lusts of their hearts, gave them up to dishonorable passions, gave them up to a debased mind. This is the shape of the wrath revealed now. It is not first fire from heaven. It is God handing us over to the very thing we chose, removing the restraint, letting the desire run to its end. The judgment is that we get what we wanted. There is no more terrifying sentence than the sound of a door not slamming but quietly opening, and God saying, very well, then, go.

**No One Reading This Is Outside It**

It is easy to read the long list at the end of chapter one as a description of other people. The murderers, the gossips, the ruthless, the heartless. We file it under them. But Paul has set a trap, and the next chapter springs it on the reader who feels superior. For now, hear the list and find yourself in it. Heartless. Boastful. Disobedient to parents. These are not exotic sins reserved for the depraved few. These are the furniture of an ordinary heart, mine included.

I have suppressed the truth this very week. I have known what God required and arranged my life to keep that knowledge submerged. I am not the prosecutor in this passage. I am the defendant.

The Christ connection comes by what is missing here. There is no gospel in this passage, only wrath revealed and excuse removed. That absence is the point. A reader who feels the full weight of being handed over to his own desire is finally ready to hear, in the chapters ahead, that God did not leave us in the hands we chose. He took our place in the wrath we earned. But not yet. First, the diagnosis must land.

We knew, and we suppressed it.

There is a particular pleasure in judging another person, and Paul knows it. He has spent a chapter describing the depravity of the pagan world, and he can feel the reader nodding along, growing comfortable, growing superior. So he turns and points straight at that nodding reader. "Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things."

**The Judge in the Dock**

This is the hinge of the whole section. The moment you feel righteous enough to condemn another, you have written your own indictment, because the standard you raised against him is the standard now raised against you. Paul is not abolishing moral judgment. He is exposing a fraud, the fraud of the person who uses the law as a weapon against others and as a shelter for himself.

He presses harder against the one who feels secure in religious privilege. To the Jew who possesses the law and the covenant sign, Paul says the possession saves no one. "For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified." Having the law is not keeping the law. Knowing the right answer is not the same as living it, and God, who "shows no partiality," does not grade on heritage. He grades on righteousness, and by that measure the religious man and the pagan man stand on the same ground.

**God Shows No Partiality**

We work hard to find a category that exempts us. The pagan thinks his ignorance excuses him, and Paul has already closed that door. The religious person thinks his knowledge protects him, and Paul closes that door too. There is no demographic of the righteous. There is no birthright that lifts a man out of the verdict. "God shows no partiality" is good news only to those who have stopped trying to be the exception.

I notice how much of my own religion is a search for the exception. I want to be the pastor who is graded on a curve, whose familiarity with Scripture counts as obedience to it. Paul will not let me have it. The man who teaches against stealing, does he steal. The man who preaches against pride, is he proud. The question is not rhetorical for me. It is a mirror.

**Every Mouth Stopped**

Then the section reaches its verdict, and Paul gathers the whole human race into one courtroom. He stacks Scripture upon Scripture, "None is righteous, no, not one; no one understands; no one seeks for God." And he tells us the purpose of all of it. "Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God."

Every mouth stopped. That is the aim. Not the mouths of the obviously wicked, but every mouth, including the mouth that loves to explain, to qualify, to plead its case. The law was never given as a ladder to climb to God. "For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin." The law's job is to silence us, to take away the speech of self-defense, to leave us with nothing to say.

The Christ connection waits just past this verse, and the silence is what prepares for it. A man with his mouth stopped is finally able to listen. The next word in Romans is "But now." Before grace can be heard as grace, the courtroom must go quiet. This passage makes it quiet.

No one is righteous, not one.

Two words change the air in the letter. After three chapters of indictment, after every mouth has been stopped and the whole world held accountable, Paul writes: "But now." Two small words, and the courtroom that had gone silent under the weight of the law hears a different voice begin to speak.

**A Righteousness Apart From the Law**

"But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the law and the prophets bear witness to it, the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe." Read what Paul does not say. He does not say God lowered the standard. He does not say the law was repealed and forgotten. He says a righteousness has been revealed apart from the law, a standing with God that does not come by climbing the ladder we already proved we cannot climb.

This righteousness is given, not achieved. It comes "for all who believe. For there is no distinction: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." The same word that flattened every claim to privilege in chapter three now flattens every claim to exclusion. No distinction in guilt becomes no distinction in the offer. The gift goes to the same place the verdict went, to everyone.

**Justified Freely by His Blood**

Then comes the heart of it. We "are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith." Three words carry the weight here, and none of them can be softened.

Justified means declared righteous, a legal verdict, the gavel coming down in our favor. Redemption means bought back, a price paid to set a slave free. Propitiation means the turning away of wrath, the wrath that chapter one said was already being revealed. Put them together and you have the gospel in a sentence. The wrath we earned fell on Christ, the price we could not pay was paid in his blood, and the verdict we dreaded was reversed.

Notice the cost. We are justified freely, as a gift, which means it costs us nothing. But it is "by his blood," which means it cost God everything. Free is never cheap. The freeness of grace to us is measured by the price of it to him.

**Just, and the Justifier**

Here is the problem Paul has been building toward, and most of us never feel its weight. How can a just God forgive the guilty without ceasing to be just. A judge who lets the guilty go free is a corrupt judge. So how does God acquit sinners and remain holy.

The cross is the answer. God "put forward" Christ "to show God's righteousness... so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus." At Calvary, justice and mercy do not compromise. Justice is satisfied because sin was punished. Mercy is extended because it was punished in our substitute. God does not wink at sin to forgive sinners. He bears it.

This is the Christ connection, and it is the whole passage. There is no gospel here apart from the blood. I am tempted, even as I preach, to want forgiveness without a cross, a God who simply overlooks. Paul will not let me have a God so unjust. The mercy I need is only as solid as the justice that paid for it.

And it leaves no room to boast. "Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded." A gift received cannot be a wage earned. The man who is justified freely has nothing left to brag about, and nothing left to fear.

Just, and the one who justifies.

If justification by faith were a new idea, an innovation Paul invented to make Christianity easier, then the whole Old Testament would stand against him. So Paul does the boldest thing he could do. He goes back to Abraham, the father of the Jewish people, the man every objector would name as the great example of righteousness, and he asks how Abraham was made right with God.

**Counted, Not Earned**

"For what does the Scripture say? 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.'" Paul fastens on a single word. Counted. Credited. It is the language of an account, of something written into a ledger. And he draws out the logic with the clarity of a man making the most important distinction in the world. "Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due. And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness."

A wage is owed. A gift is given. If Abraham earned his righteousness, then God was paying a debt, and there is no grace in paying what you owe. But Abraham did not earn it. He believed, and the righteousness was credited to his account as a gift. Notice who God justifies in that sentence. He "justifies the ungodly." Not the righteous. Not the deserving. The ungodly. Abraham is counted righteous precisely as a man who was not.

**Before the Sign, Before the Law**

Then Paul presses the timeline, and the timeline wins the argument. When was Abraham counted righteous. Before or after he was circumcised. "How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised." The righteousness came first. The sign came later, as a seal of a righteousness he already had by faith.

This is not a small point. It means Abraham is the father of all who believe, circumcised or not, Jew or Gentile. The promise never ran through the ritual. It ran through faith, and it ran through faith before any law was given. "For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith." If the inheritance depended on law-keeping, faith would be empty and the promise void. Paul stakes everything on the order of events, and the order of events is grace before works, every time.

**The God Who Raises the Dead**

What kind of faith was it. Not a vague optimism. Abraham believed a specific thing about a specific God. He was a hundred years old, his body as good as dead, Sarah's womb barren, and "no unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God, fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised." He trusted "the God who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist."

That is the bridge to Christ, and Paul builds it himself. "It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification." The same God who brought life from Abraham's dead body brought life from the tomb. The faith that justified Abraham and the faith that justifies us are the same faith in the same God, a God who creates out of nothing and raises the dead.

I find my own faith wants a contribution. I want to add something, a work, a record, a sign I can point to. Abraham strips that away. He was counted righteous with nothing to show but a body too old to produce an heir, trusting a God who specializes in the impossible. My empty hands are not a problem for this gospel. They are the only qualification.

Counted righteous before he worked.

Justified. Declared righteous. The verdict has come down. And the first thing Paul says about life on the far side of that verdict is the thing we most need and least believe. "Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." Not a truce. Not a ceasefire that could break at any moment. Peace. The war is over, and it is over because the verdict is final.

**Peace That Does Not Depend on Us**

We struggle to believe this because our peace with God has always felt conditional, rising and falling with our performance. A good week, and we feel close. A bad week, and we feel the distance return. Paul cuts that cord. The peace is grounded "through our Lord Jesus Christ," not through our consistency. "Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand."

We stand in grace. We do not visit it on our better days. It is the ground under our feet, and the ground does not shift when we do. This is why Paul can do the unthinkable next thing, which is to "rejoice in our sufferings." Not because suffering is good, but because the peace is so secure that even suffering cannot threaten it, and instead produces endurance, character, and hope. Hope, Paul says, "does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts."

**While We Were Still Sinners**

Then comes the verse that measures the love. "For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly." And again, lest we miss it, "but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." Read the timing. Not after we cleaned ourselves up. Not once we showed promise. While we were still sinners. While we were still enemies, Paul says a few verses later. The cross was not God's response to our improvement. It was God's love aimed at us at our worst.

This is where I have to stop and let it indict my picture of God. I keep imagining a God who waited for me to become worth loving. Paul says God moved while I was unlovable, while I was an enemy, and that the proof of his love is not how I turned out but what Christ did when I had turned out badly. If God loved me there, in the place of my rebellion, then nothing I do now can earn a love I never earned in the first place, and nothing I do can lose it either.

**Two Men, Two Humanities**

The second half of the chapter pulls back to show the largest possible frame. Paul sets two men side by side, and all of humanity hangs on one or the other. Adam and Christ. "Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned." One man's trespass put the whole race under condemnation. We were born into Adam's failure, inheriting a death we did not personally commit.

But over against the first Adam stands the second. "For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous." This is the architecture of salvation. We are not saved by improving Adam's record. We are transferred into another man's record entirely, the obedience of Christ counted to us the way Adam's disobedience was counted to us.

And grace runs further than sin ever did. "Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more." There is no sin so deep that grace does not reach deeper. That is not a license, as the next chapter will insist. It is the floor beneath the believer, the assurance that the second Adam's obedience outweighs everything the first Adam left us.

Where sin increased, grace abounded more.

Paul has just said something dangerous, and he knows it. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more. A clever mind hears that and draws the obvious conclusion. Then let us sin more, so grace can abound more. Paul names the thought and recoils from it. "What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means."

**You Cannot Live in What You Died To**

His answer is not a rule. It is a fact about who we now are. "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" The argument turns on a death that has already happened. In baptism, Paul says, we were joined to Christ's death. "We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life."

This is the logic the whole chapter rests on. The believer is not a sinner trying hard to quit. The believer is a person who has died to one life and been raised into another. The old self "was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin." The chain is broken, not merely loosened. A dead man owes sin nothing.

**Reckon It True**

So what do we do with a death that has already happened. Paul gives a command, and the command is mostly a matter of belief. "So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus." Consider. Reckon. Count it as true, because it is true. The first work of holiness is to believe what God has already declared about you.

Then the will engages. "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions." And here Paul speaks directly to the hands and the body. "Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life." Present. It is a daily, deliberate handing over. The body that once served sin is now to be placed, member by member, in the service of God. Sin no longer has dominion, not because temptation stops, but "since you are not under law but under grace."

I have to be honest about how I have read this. I have used grace as a quiet permission, treating the freeness of forgiveness as room to keep the sin I was comfortable with. Paul cuts that off at the root. Grace is not the freedom to keep sinning. It is the power that broke sin's reign. To go on serving what I died to is not to enjoy grace. It is to deny it.

**Slaves of One or the Other**

The chapter ends by stripping away the illusion of neutrality. There is no third option, no autonomous self that serves no master. "You are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness." We were slaves of sin. We have been "set free from sin and have become slaves of righteousness." Freedom, in Paul's hands, is not the absence of a master. It is the right master, the one whose service is life.

Then the verdict on the two slaveries, in a verse no one forgets. "For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." Wages and gift, again. Sin pays what it owes, and what it owes is death. God gives what we could never earn, and what he gives is life. The Christ connection is the hinge: it is in him that we died, in him we were raised, in him the gift is given. We did not break our own chains. He did, and now we live as people already free.

You died. Now live like it.

Every honest believer knows the experience even if they cannot explain it. You want to do the good thing. You decide to do it. And you find yourself doing the opposite, watching as if from a distance while your own hands betray your own intentions. Romans 7 is the chapter where Paul takes that experience seriously, and refuses to blame the law for it.

**The Law Is Holy, and It Cannot Save**

Paul has a problem. He has said we are no longer under law but under grace, and he has implied the law stirs sin. So does that make the law evil. "What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means." The law is not the villain. "So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good." The trouble is not the law's character. The trouble is what the law meets when it arrives, which is us.

The commandment says do not covet, and the very prohibition awakens the desire. "For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness." This is the strange power of a boundary. Tell a heart already bent toward sin that a thing is forbidden, and the heart wants it more. The law did not create the sin. It exposed it, named it, and in naming it provoked it. The law is a mirror that shows the disease. It was never the medicine.

**The War Inside**

Then Paul opens his own chest and lets us see the conflict. "For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate." Read that as a confession, not a theory. "For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing."

There is a long argument about whether Paul describes his life before Christ or after. I will not settle it from this pulpit, and I do not think the comfort depends on settling it. What I know is that the war Paul describes is the war I am in. The wanting and the failing, living in the same chest, in the same hour. The man who delights in the law of God in his inner being and finds another law at work in his members, "waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive."

I confess this is the chapter that keeps me honest. There are days I preach holiness and go home and lose the war by dinner. The temptation is to pretend, to present a self that has it handled. Paul will not let me pretend. He, the apostle, names the failure out loud, and in naming it he tells the truth about every Christian still in the body. The war is not a sign you are not saved. It is the mark of a person who finally sees clearly, who wants the good with a will the old self never had, and still falls.

**The Cry and the Answer**

The chapter does not end in despair, but it travels through despair to get to its hope. Paul cries out, "Who will deliver me from this body of death?" That is the cry the law was always meant to produce. Not pride in keeping it, but a cry for rescue from a self that cannot keep it. The law brings you to the end of yourself, and the end of yourself is the only place the gospel can begin.

"Wretched man that I am," he writes, and then, before the argument is even finished, the answer breaks in. "Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord." There is the Christ connection, and it is everything. The deliverance the law could never give comes through a person, not a program. The war is real, and it is not yet over, but the deliverer has already come, and chapter eight will tell us there is now no condemnation. First the cry. Then the name.

Who will deliver me from this body.

There is no condemnation. Read it again, because everything in the Christian life leans on it. "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." After the war of chapter seven, after the cry of the wretched man, this is the answer arriving in full. Not less condemnation. Not condemnation deferred. No condemnation, now, for those in Christ.

**Life in the Spirit, Not Death in the Flesh**

Why no condemnation. Because the work was done elsewhere. "For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh." The condemnation did not vanish. It fell, on Christ, in his body, so that it could never fall on those who are his. The law could not give life because it met sinful flesh. So God sent his Son into that very flesh, and there, on the cross, the verdict was carried out.

Now the Spirit who raised Christ lives in the believer, and that changes the whole register of life. "You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you." This is not a higher tier of Christian reserved for the spiritually elite. It is the ordinary condition of everyone in Christ. The same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead "will also give life to your mortal bodies." The resurrection is not only behind us in Christ. It is ahead of us, promised to our own bodies, guaranteed by the Spirit already at work.

**Adopted, and Heirs**

Then Paul names what we have become, and the word is family. "For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons," the Spirit by whom we cry out to God as Abba, Father. The relationship is not that of a frightened servant kept at a distance. It is a child crying out to a father with the most intimate word. And if children, then heirs, "heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ."

This is where the chapter widens to take in all of suffering. The present sufferings are real, and Paul does not minimize them. But "the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us." The whole creation groans, we groan, and the Spirit himself groans within us, interceding "with groanings too deep for words." We are not abandoned to our weakness in prayer. The Spirit prays underneath our broken prayers.

I notice how rarely I live as though any of this were true. I carry the fear of a slave, not the freedom of a son. I pray as though God were reluctant, as though I had to argue him into mercy, when in fact the Spirit is already interceding for me according to the will of God. The problem is not that the inheritance is uncertain. The problem is that I keep falling back into fear God has already cast out.

**Nothing Can Separate Us**

Then the chapter rises to the highest ground in the letter. "And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good." Not all things are good. But all things are worked, by a God who is for us, toward a good he has already determined, an unbreakable chain from foreknowledge to glorification. "If God is for us, who can be against us?"

And the final question answers itself. "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?" Paul lists the worst the world can do, tribulation, distress, persecution, death, and then declares: "neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come... will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord." The love is in Christ, secured by his death and resurrection, held by the God who did not spare his own Son. That is the Christ connection, and it is the foundation of all assurance. The love that will not let us go is not our grip on him. It is his grip on us.

Nothing can separate us from him.

Paul has just finished saying that nothing can separate us from the love of God. And then, almost in the same breath, he writes the most sorrowful words in the letter. "I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh." The question that breaks his heart is this: if God's promises are so secure, why has Israel, the people of the promise, largely rejected her Messiah. Has the word of God failed.

**The Word Has Not Failed**

That is the question driving these three chapters, and Paul answers it at once. "But it is not as though the word of God has failed." The promise never guaranteed every physical descendant. "For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel." From the beginning, God's purpose ran through election, not lineage. Isaac, not Ishmael. Jacob, not Esau. The line of promise was always God's choosing, not man's bloodline, so the unbelief of many does not break a promise that was never made to all.

This raises the hardest question in the chapter, and Paul does not soften it. "He has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills." We recoil. We want to put God in the dock. Paul anticipates exactly that. "Who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, 'Why have you made me like this?'" This is not a tidy answer. It is a larger God. Paul refuses to make divine mercy small enough for us to control. Mercy that I can earn or demand is not mercy. It is wages.

**Mercy Through Israel's Stumbling**

But Paul does not leave Israel's hardening as the end of the story. Their stumbling has a purpose, and the purpose is mercy reaching further. "Through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles." Israel's no opened the door to the nations. And Paul, himself a Jew, will not let the Gentiles grow proud about it.

He gives them the image of the olive tree. The natural branches were broken off, and wild branches, the Gentiles, were grafted in. But the grafted branch has nothing to boast about. "Do not become proud, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you." The Gentile stands in the tree by mercy alone, on the same terms as everyone else, and a branch that forgets that is a branch inviting the same axe.

I feel the rebuke in this, because I am one of the wild branches, a Gentile grafted into a promise that was not first mine. The temptation of every latecomer to grace is to forget he was a latecomer, to look at those broken off and feel secure rather than humbled. Paul gives me fear, not as terror, but as the proper posture of a man who knows he is held by kindness he did not produce and cannot maintain.

**Mercy on All**

Then Paul lifts his eyes to the end, and what he sees is not Israel cast off forever but Israel's hardening as partial and temporary. "A partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved." The God who hardened has not abandoned. The same sovereign mercy that grafted in the Gentiles will yet show mercy to the natural branches. "For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all."

That is the resolution. Not that some deserved mercy and some did not, but that all were disobedient and mercy is the only door for anyone. The Christ connection runs underneath the whole argument: the Messiah Israel stumbled over is the same Christ in whom Gentiles are grafted in, and the mercy of God for both Jew and Gentile flows from one rejected, risen Lord. Paul ends not with an explanation but with worship, marveling at the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God, declaring how unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways. When the argument reaches the edge of what we can understand, the right response is not protest. It is praise.

Mercy belongs to God alone.

For eleven chapters Paul has been telling us what God has done. The verb has been God's. He justified, he sent his Son, he poured out his Spirit, he showed mercy. And now, at chapter twelve, the letter turns, and it turns on a single word: therefore. "I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God." Everything Paul is about to ask flows from everything God has already given. The ethics rest on the mercies, never the reverse.

**A Body Offered**

The first command is total. "I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship." Notice the strangeness of it. A living sacrifice. A sacrifice was, by definition, killed. Paul asks for one that stays on the altar and goes on living, an offering renewed every morning, a body handed over while it still breathes.

And it is the body, not merely the soul. The hands, the schedule, the appetites, the tongue. Christianity is not a private feeling that leaves the body to itself. The mercy that saved the whole person claims the whole person. This is the only fitting response to grace. Not a payment, since grace cannot be repaid, but an offering, a life laid down because a life was first laid down for us.

**A Mind Made New**

Then comes the inward command, and it is the engine of the rest. "Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect." There are two forces pressing on the believer. The world presses from outside, pouring us into its mold by sheer repetition until its assumptions feel like ours. Against that, God works from inside, by the renewal of the mind.

The will of God is not discerned by a passive heart. It is discerned by a renewed mind, a mind retrained until it can tell the genuine good from the counterfeit. I confess how little of my own thinking has actually been renewed. I have let the world set my instincts about success, about anger, about who deserves my attention, and then I have asked God to bless instincts that came straight from the mold I was supposed to be broken out of. Renewal is slow, and it is the daily work I most often skip.

What does the renewed life look like. Paul gets concrete fast. "Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good." Outdo one another in showing honor. Bless those who persecute you. "Repay no one evil for evil." So far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all. This is the living sacrifice in motion, love that refuses revenge and leaves vengeance to God.

**Owe No One Anything, Except Love**

Chapter thirteen presses the offered body into the public square. The Christian submits to governing authorities, "for there is no authority except from God." We pay our taxes, we give honor where it is owed, not because the state is sacred but because God orders the world through it. And then Paul gathers the whole law into one debt that can never be paid off. "Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law." Every other debt you can clear. This one you carry forever, because love is never finished.

The chapter ends with the clock. "The hour has come for you to wake from sleep... the night is far gone; the day is at hand." And the final command is a person. "Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh." There is the Christ connection, and it closes the circle. We began by being clothed in Christ's righteousness as a gift, and now we are told to put on Christ as a garment for daily living, to wear the One who saved us. The indicative becomes the imperative. What God made us, we now live out.

Mercy received becomes a body offered.

Every church has them, and most churches divide over them. The questions where Scripture does not draw a clear line and sincere believers land in different places. In Rome it was food and days, whether a Christian could eat meat that may have touched idol worship, whether one day was holier than another. Paul calls these the disputable things, and he spends a chapter and a half teaching a church how to stay one church across them.

**Stop Despising, Stop Judging**

Paul names two sins, one for each side, and they mirror each other. "As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions." The strong believer, free in conscience, is tempted to despise the scrupulous one as a lightweight. The weak believer, careful in conscience, is tempted to judge the free one as a compromiser. "Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him."

The argument that disarms both sides is the same. Each believer answers to God, not to the other. "Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls." You are not the Lord of your brother's conscience. He has a Master, and it is not you. "For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God." When I remember that my brother answers to God and not to me, my urge to police him loses its footing. I have a judgment seat of my own to prepare for, and it will not ask me how well I corrected him.

**Love Restrains Liberty**

Then Paul says something that cuts against everything we believe about rights. He grants that the strong are right. "I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself." The strong believer has the better theology. And then Paul tells him to set his rightness aside for the sake of love. "If your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died."

Read that last line slowly. The one for whom Christ died. Paul measures your brother by the cross, not by his weak conscience. If Christ thought him worth dying for, your freedom to eat is a small thing to surrender for his sake. "So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding." Liberty is real, but love is higher, and the mature use of freedom is often the willing limiting of it.

I have used my freedom as a weapon, insisting on my rights at the table while a weaker brother stumbled, and called it principle. Paul calls it a failure to walk in love. The question is not whether I am free. The question is whether my freedom builds my brother up or knocks him down, and too often I have wanted to be right more than I have wanted him to stand.

**Welcome as Christ Welcomed You**

Paul does not leave us with mere tolerance. He gives us the pattern, and the pattern is a person. "Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God." Here is the Christ connection, and it governs the whole chapter. How did Christ welcome us. Not after we had our consciences sorted out. Not once we were strong. He welcomed us as we were, weak and wrong and unclean, and bore with our failings at the cost of his life. "For Christ did not please himself."

That is the standard. The strong are to bear with the weak the way Christ bore with all of us, who were weak together. A church that welcomes only the people who already agree on every disputable thing has forgotten how it was welcomed in the first place. We were received by sheer grace, and grace received is meant to become grace extended, across the table, over the very things we are sure we are right about.

Welcome each other as Christ welcomed you.
